description: Stand behind a line, swing, and jump as far as your body allows. That distance is not a leg-size report, it is a hip power measurement, and it predicts your sprint better than any mirror. Measure yours, learn what drives it, and start training the engine behind it.

beats.text: A LINE AND A TAPE MEASURE

scenes.narration: Today your whole gym is a line on the ground and something to measure with: a tape, a ruler, two shoes placed heel to heel, anything honest. Stand with your toes behind the line, feet hip width. Swing your arms back, sink into a quarter squat, then explode: arms forward, hips through, jump as far as you can and stick the landing on both feet. Measure from the line to the back of your nearest heel, because the heel that lands shortest is the truth. Three attempts, best distance counts, and that distance in centimeters is your number today. Keep it safe somewhere. The mirror has been grading your legs by how they look in shorts. This tape grades them by what they can actually do, and the grade is written by one system most skinny guys never train on purpose: the power stored in your hips. By the end I will show you exactly what your distance says about that system, and the honest news is that hip power is one of the fastest qualities in your whole body to build.

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN SOFT AND SPRINGY
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Two meters is where an untrained jump becomes an athletic one. Under one meter sixty, your hips are simply unpracticed at exploding, and unpracticed is the most fixable diagnosis in this entire season. Between one sixty and two meters, the engine works but fires late and soft. Over two meters forty, you own horizontal power that most bigger guys cannot buy with size, because jump distance is not really about force. It is about force divided by the bodyweight that force must move, and that division is where your frame quietly wins. A heavy jumper must produce enormous force just to match your ratio. You start the race with the math already tilted toward you, and the rest of this episode is about collecting on it.
scenes.sub: under 1.6 m: untrained hips - over 2.4 m: elite horizontal power

lines: Glutes are the largest muscle you own.
The jump is their report card.
beats.title: THE ENGINE IS THE HIP

scenes.narration: Look at the hip joint, because the broad jump is mostly a hip event wearing a jump costume. When you sink into the countermovement, you load three springs at once: ankle, knee and hip, a chain called triple extension. But the shares are not equal. The hip extensors, your glutes, are the largest and strongest muscle group in your entire body, and in a horizontal jump they deliver the biggest share of the blast, driving your pelvis forward and up while the quads and calves finish the job at the ground. Think of the jump as a door being thrown open: the calves are the handle, but the hip is the hinge and the arm throwing it. This is why some lean guys jump freakishly far with unimpressive legs. Their hinge is strong and fast, and the tape measure only ever sees the result of the hinge. Size sits in the mirror. Power sits in the hip.

The science word for what the tape measures is rate of force development: how much force you can produce in the first fraction of a second. A broad jump gives you roughly a quarter of a second on the ground to build your blast. A muscle can be enormous and still useless here if it arrives slowly, which is why bodybuilders with tree-trunk legs often jump ordinary distances, and why wiry sprinters fly. Your nervous system decides how many muscle fibers fire in that window and how fast they climb to full force. Jump distance also tracks sprint speed remarkably well in testing, because the first steps of a sprint are the same horizontal hip blast, repeated. Train the jump and you are secretly training your start. Your distance today is a photograph of your nervous system's firing speed, taken through your hips.

beats.text: THROW THE ARMS, THEN THE HIPS

scenes.narration: One deep-dive detail before we train, because it is free distance most guys leave on the floor: your arms. A full, aggressive arm swing, back as you sink and violently forward as you jump, adds roughly ten to fifteen percent to broad jump distance in lab testing. The swing loads the hips harder on the way down and pulls your center of mass forward in the air. The other free detail is depth: a quarter squat, not a deep squat. Sink too deep and the blast window stretches and softens; stay tall and quick, like you are bouncing off hot ground. And land tall enough to stick it: chest up, heels down, no falling backward, because a fall backward is measured at the hand, not the heel, and hands are expensive.

Your advantage in this test is pure physics, and physics does not care about your feelings. Jump distance is force divided by mass, and every kilo a bigger guy carries is cargo his force must drag through the air. You produce force with muscles that are, kilo for kilo, just as capable as his, and then you spend that force on a lighter body. This is why the jump events have always belonged to lean athletes: the tape rewards the ratio, never the bulk. It is also why your ceiling here is genuinely high. A skinny guy who trains his hinge seriously is not hoping to catch the big jumpers. He is built in the shape that jumping prefers, and most of his heavier rivals are training against their own geometry. You are training with yours.

Now we jump together. Four rounds: twenty seconds of broad jumps, full arm swing, stick every landing, walk back and reset. Rest forty seconds between rounds. Power is built fresh, never tired, so every rep should look like your best one.

beats.text: JUMP TWICE A WEEK, ALWAYS FRESH
FIVE PERFECT REPS BEAT TWENTY SLOPPY

scenes.narration: Your protocol for the next thirty days. Jump twice a week, always fresh, never the day after heavy leg work, because power trained tired becomes slow work and slow work teaches slowness. Five sets of three perfect broad jumps, full rest, full swing, stick the landing, done. Between jump days, feed the engine: hip hinge work like Romanian deadlift patterns with a backpack or heavy object, three sets, slow down, explosive up, teaches the glutes to produce the force the jump spends. Sprint once a week if you can, even twenty meters, because the start and the jump are cousins. And protect the landings: soft ground, quiet feet, because the springs you land on are the same ones we spent this season protecting. Small menu, honest work, thirty days.

So, your distance. Under one meter sixty: your hips are unwired, not weak, and this is the band with the fastest gains in the whole season, because the engine exists and only the firing is missing. One sixty to two meters: the system works; technique and hinge strength will walk you over the line within a couple of months. Two meters to two forty: trained power, the neighborhood where sprinters live. Over two forty: elite horizontal pop for a bodyweight athlete, protect it and build on it. Put your distance in the comments, just the number, and retest in thirty days: same line, same shoes, same honest heel. The tape does not do compliments. It does progress.

Thirty days from now, same line, same tape, bring me a longer jump and we will talk about what it did to your sprint. Subscribe, and keep your number safe until then. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Your Broad Jump Distance Reveals the Truth About Your hip power
